The idea in plain words. A typical WLAN is just an extension of your Ethernet LAN. Wireless hosts still have MAC addresses and IP addresses, and the access point (AP) connects them to the wired network. The big difference: wireless is half-duplex. Everyone shares the same channel and only one device talks at a time, like Ethernet with a hub. BOOK pp549-551
| Type | Range (book Figure 19.2) | Example | Notes |
| WPAN (personal area) | Under about 5 to 10 meters (about 30 feet max) | Bluetooth: mouse, keyboard, headset | Low power, unlicensed, short reach |
| WLAN (local area) | Under about 100 meters | Wi-Fi in homes, offices | Most popular today, unlicensed band |
| WMAN (metro area) | Over 100 meters, a city or campus | Building-to-building wireless links | Needs line of sight; cheaper than leased lines |
| WWAN (wide area) | Cities and beyond | Cellular data | Provider-owned; usually slower than WLAN |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's WLAN speeds (11 Mbps for 802.11b, 54 Mbps for 802.11g/a) are history. Today's networks use 802.11n, 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5), 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6 and 6E) and 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7). The book's WWAN discussion (TV adverts, "latest cellular networks") is also dated; think 4G and 5G. UPDATED CHECK (general knowledge; not looked up)
Quick check 19.1
Q1. Which wireless network type is Bluetooth?
Answer: WPAN - Personal area network.
Q2. Why is a WLAN compared to Ethernet with hubs?
Answer: It is half-duplex: all devices share one channel and only one transmits at a time - A switch gives each port its own collision domain; an AP does not.
Q3. Which wireless type needs line of sight between sites?
Answer: WMAN (wireless bridges between buildings) - Fiber is better if available.
Q4. Do WLAN users pay to use the radio frequency band?
Answer: No, it is an unlicensed band - Same for PANs.
A basic WLAN needs only two things: a wireless access point and a wireless network interface card (NIC) in each client. BOOK p553
19.2.1 Wireless Access Points
- An AP is the central point for wireless stations, like a hub or switch in a wired network. Because wireless is half-duplex, the hub comparison is the more accurate one. BOOK
- It has at least one antenna, usually two (diversity), and a port to the wired network.
- It works as a bridge between wireless clients and the wired network.
- SoHo devices are either a stand-alone AP or a wireless router (often with NAT and DHCP built in).
- The wired connection behind the AP is the distribution system (DS). 802.11 frames can carry up to four MAC addresses, but only when a wireless DS is in use. BOOK
- The AP keeps an association table: a list of connected stations by MAC address. BOOK
Autonomous and lightweight APs [BOOK]
| Type | How it is managed | Good and bad |
| Autonomous AP | Configured and managed on its own, one by one | Simple for one or two APs; hard to manage many |
| Lightweight AP | Gets its configuration from a wireless LAN controller (WLC); the AP acts mostly as the radio and antenna | Central management, easier roaming. Needs a WLC |
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
Lightweight APs and the WLC talk using CAPWAP (a tunnel protocol). The book names LWAPP; see the update in section 19.3.8. WLC models, AP modes and setup are in Chapter 20. ADDED
19.2.2 Wireless Network Interface Card (NIC)

A wireless NIC does the same job as a normal NIC, but it has a radio antenna instead of a cable port. Nearly all laptops have one built in. External cards are only used for poor reception areas or network analyzers. BOOK p555
19.2.3 Wireless Antennas
| Antenna class | Also called | Pattern | Use |
| Omni-directional | Point-to-multipoint | Spreads power in all directions, like a donut | Most APs: clients can be anywhere |
| Directional (for example Yagi) | Point-to-point | Focuses power in one direction | Longer range in one direction; must be aimed carefully |
A Yagi reaches farther than an omni of the same gain because it concentrates the power. The downside is precise alignment. BOOK p556
Quick check 19.2
Q1. What is the wired side of an AP called?
Answer: The distribution system (DS) - It also carries MAC information for the 802.11 frames.
Q2. Which type of AP gets its configuration from a WLC?
Answer: Lightweight AP - Autonomous APs are configured individually.
Q3. Which antenna type usually gives the longest range in one direction?
Answer: Directional (Yagi) - It focuses the power.
Q4. Why do most APs use omni antennas?
Answer: Clients can be in any direction - A directional antenna would miss most of them.
The book lists the network types you will meet: IBSS, BSS, ESS, workgroup bridges, repeater APs, bridging (point-to-point and point-to-multipoint) and mesh. BOOK p556
| Term | Meaning in one line |
| IBSS (ad hoc) | Devices talk directly with no AP |
| BSS | One AP and its clients: the coverage cell |
| ESS | Two or more APs with the same SSID, joined by the wired DS, so users can roam |
| Repeater AP | Extends coverage by repeating a signal; no wired connection |
| Bridge | Links two wired LANs wirelessly (root and non-root) |
| Mesh | APs connect to each other by radio, with many redundant paths |
19.3.1 Independent Basic Service Set (Ad Hoc)

Wireless devices talk directly with no AP. Two laptops with wireless NICs in ad hoc mode are enough. The network exists as soon as two devices communicate, and it works at about 20 to 40 meters. It is also called peer to peer. It does not scale, it is insecure, and the book recommends turning ad hoc mode off before connecting to the wired network. BOOK pp556-557
19.3.2 Basic Service Set (BSS)
A BSS is the area, or cell, covered by one AP. It is also called the basic service area (BSA). The AP manages all connections, so it scales better than ad hoc. BOOK p557
19.3.3 Infrastructure Basic Service Set

In infrastructure mode clients talk only to the AP, never directly to each other, and the AP connects to the wired network through the DS. To the rest of the network the wireless clients look like normal wired hosts. Basic stand-alone APs talk to each other only through the DS, not by radio. BOOK pp558-559
19.3.4 Service Set ID

The SSID is the name of a wireless network. It is a sequence of 1 to 32 octets (usually readable text). It can be broadcast (shows in the client's list) or hidden (the client needs a saved profile). BOOK p559
- The AP ties each SSID to a MAC address: the radio's own MAC is the BSSID. If one AP has several SSIDs, each gets a virtual MAC (an MBSSID). BOOK

- Several SSIDs do not speed up anything and do not split collision or broadcast domains. They share the same half-duplex radio. Their purpose is different security levels for different groups, for example Sales and Contractor. BOOK
COMMON MISTAKE

The book often treats SSID and BSS as the same thing. They are not. The SSID is a name (it can cover many APs), and a BSS is one AP's cell, identified by its BSSID (the AP radio's MAC address). Many people mix them up in conversation, so know both meanings. UPDATED CHECK (IEEE 802.11 terms; not re-read in the standard in this session)
A hidden SSID is not real security. The name is still sent in some frames and is easy to find. Use proper encryption instead. ADDED CHECK
19.3.5 Extended Service Set

If you give all APs the same SSID, mobile clients can roam from one AP to the next without losing the connection. This is the most common corporate design. It is an extended service set (ESS). BOOK pp560-561
- Neighboring cells should overlap by about 20 percent so users do not lose the signal. BOOK Figure 19.8 and text
- The neighboring APs must use different channels (the figure uses channels 1 and 6), or they will interfere. BOOK
COMMON MISTAKE

The book contradicts itself: the text says overlap at least 20 percent, but review question 18 uses 15 percent in its correct answer. Both are rules of thumb. For the exam, if a question says "at least 15 percent", that is the right answer to that question; otherwise remember 15 to 20 percent. UPDATED CHECK
19.3.6 Repeaters

A repeater AP is not connected to the wired network. It receives the signal from a wired AP and repeats it to far-away clients. For each repeater you lose about half the throughput, so use repeaters only for low-bandwidth devices such as warehouse barcode readers. A dual-radio repeater (one radio receives, one transmits) works like a dual half-duplex repeater. BOOK p561
19.3.7 Bridging

Wireless bridges join two or more wired LANs, usually in different buildings, into one LAN at Layer 2. They have no routing, so you need a router for different IP subnets. Bridges make the broadcast domain bigger. BOOK p562
- Point-to-point: two buildings joined, often outdoors.
- Point-to-multipoint: a main building linked to several remote buildings. The remote buildings cannot talk directly to each other; they must go through the central point.
Root and non-root rules [BOOK]
| Rule | Detail |
| Non-root devices talk only to root devices | Non-root devices: non-root bridges, workgroup bridges, repeater APs, wireless clients |
| Root devices cannot talk to other root devices | Root devices: APs and bridges connected to the wired network |
| Non-root devices cannot talk to other non-root devices | Exception: a non-root bridge acting as a two-radio repeater can link to another non-root bridge if one of them has a root bridge uplink |
19.3.8 Mesh Networks

In a mesh, each device only needs to reach the next one, and devices repeat traffic for others. Many redundant paths make it reliable and fault tolerant, so a failed node is simply routed around. Paths change with traffic, radio conditions and priority. Mesh is expensive and aimed at large or outdoor areas. BOOK pp564-565
COMMON MISTAKE

The book says the IETF's "latest draft", LWAPP, governs how lightweight APs communicate with the WLAN system. That is out of date. LWAPP was documented as informational RFC 5412, and the standards-track replacement is CAPWAP, RFC 5415 (with the 802.11 binding in RFC 5416). CAPWAP uses UDP ports 5246 (control) and 5247 (data). Cisco controllers use CAPWAP. UPDATED (RFC Editor pages are official; the UDP port numbers come from a Wikipedia article, secondary.) CHECK
Quick check 19.3
Q1. Two laptops connect directly with no AP. What is this topology called?
Answer: IBSS (ad hoc) - Review question 16 in the book.
Q2. How long can an SSID be?
Answer: 1 to 32 octets (up to 32 characters) - The book: sequence of 1 to 32 octets.
Q3. Why create several SSIDs on one AP?
Answer: To give different groups different security settings - It does not improve performance.
Q4. To let users roam without disconnecting, what must be true of the SSID and the channels?
Answer: Same SSID on all APs, different channels on neighboring APs - That creates an ESS.
Q5. How much throughput does each repeater cost?
Answer: About half - Use repeaters only for low-bandwidth devices.
Q6. Can two root bridges talk to each other?
Answer: No - Root devices only talk to non-root devices.

The idea in plain words. Wi-Fi channels are slices of radio spectrum. If two APs near each other use the same or overlapping channels, they interfere and everyone slows down. So you choose channels that do not overlap. This is exam objective v1.1 1.11.a and v2.0 1.5.a. BOOK p565
19.4.1 2.4GHz Band
- The 2.4 GHz band (the ISM band) is used by 802.11, 802.11b and 802.11g. BOOK
- Channels approved: 11 in the United States, 13 in Europe, 14 in Japan. BOOK
- Each channel is about 22 MHz wide, but the center frequencies are only 5 MHz apart, so neighboring channels overlap heavily. BOOK
- In the US only channels 1, 6 and 11 are non-overlapping. BOOK
VERIFY

Script check. Center frequency = 2407 + 5 x channel number (MHz). Channels 1 and 6 are 25 MHz apart, so with 22 MHz width they do not overlap. Channels 1 and 5 are 20 MHz apart, so they do overlap. Searching all channels 1 to 11, the only set of three non-overlapping channels is 1, 6, 11 (no set of four exists). ADDED CHECK (center-frequency formula is general knowledge)
What happens when APs overlap [BOOK]
| Situation | What happens | Result |
| Same channel | The APs hear each other and take turns (using the duration field in the frame header) | Both networks slower: they share the airtime |
| One or two channels apart | They cannot hear each other well enough to defer, so they transmit at the same time | Collisions and retransmissions: usually worse |
EXAM CRITICAL

Both cases end in lower throughput. Same channel is the better of the two bad choices. For several APs in the 2.4 GHz band use 1, 6, 11. The book's wording "at least four channels' space between them" means four channels in between, for example 1 and 6. BOOK UPDATED
19.4.2 5GHz Band
- 802.11a uses the 5 GHz band, split into the UNII bands (Unlicensed National Information Infrastructure). BOOK
- Channel numbers in the book: UNII-1: 36, 40, 44, 48. UNII-2: 52, 56, 60, 64. UNII-3: 149, 153, 157, 161. BOOK
- 5 GHz has more non-overlapping channels than 2.4 GHz, so it is easier to plan. BOOK
COMMON MISTAKE

The book says that in the lower UNII band the center points are 10 MHz apart and in the other two bands 20 MHz apart. That is wrong. Script check: channels 36, 40, 44, 48 have centers 5180, 5200, 5220, 5240 MHz, which is 20 MHz apart. Sources confirm 20 MHz spacing across the 5 GHz band. UPDATED (A Cisco design guide and secondary sites; also see the book's own Figure 19.14.)
The book also leaves out the middle UNII channels 100 to 144 and channel 165. Channels 52 to 64 and 100 to 144 need DFS (radar detection). ADDED CHECK (secondary sources)
| Band | Width of each channel | Spacing | Non-overlapping channels |
| 2.4 GHz | About 22 MHz (DSSS) | 5 MHz | 3 in the US: 1, 6, 11 |
| 5 GHz | 20 MHz | 20 MHz | All 20 MHz channels (many) |
Using several APs in one area [BOOK]
- Reasons for several APs: many users in a small area (fewer clients per AP), or an area bigger than one AP can cover (and you want roaming).
- In 2.4 GHz choose channels with enough space between them (1, 6, 11) and reuse them in a pattern so that cells using the same channel never touch (Figure 19.15, channel 6 used eight times).
- In 5 GHz the book says two cells should separate cells that use the same channel (Figure 19.16).
802.11n (2.4 and 5 GHz) [BOOK] p569
This part has no row of its own in the book's contents list. 802.11n adds MIMO (many transmit and receive antennas) and works in both bands. The book names three main improvements: BOOK
- 40 MHz channels: two 20 MHz channels combined for more throughput.
- MAC efficiency (block acknowledgment): many frames are acknowledged together instead of one at a time.
- MIMO and spatial multiplexing: several frames sent by several antennas over several paths, then recombined. It is designed to be backward compatible with a, b and g.
COMMON MISTAKE

The book's arithmetic (54 Mbps doubled to 108, plus 11 Mbps of side tones to give "119 Mbps", script check: 54 x 2 + 11 = 119) is a rough illustration only. Real 802.11n rates depend on the number of streams and the channel width. UPDATED CHECK The book also says 802.11n allows up to eight antennas; most APs use four to six. BOOK
Wi-Fi generations [ADDED]
| Standard | Wi-Fi name | Band(s) |
| 802.11n | Wi-Fi 4 | 2.4 and 5 GHz |
| 802.11ac | Wi-Fi 5 | 5 GHz |
| 802.11ax | Wi-Fi 6 (6E adds 6 GHz) | 2.4 and 5 GHz; 6 GHz with 6E |
| 802.11be | Wi-Fi 7 | 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz |
VERIFY

This generation table is general knowledge and was not looked up in this session. Cisco's v2.0 objective 1.5.a says band and channel selection, so expect 6 GHz to matter. The Wi-Fi 1/2/3 names are informal. CHECK
Quick check 19.4
Q1. Which 2.4 GHz channels are non-overlapping in the US?
Answer: 1, 6 and 11 - Script check: no set of four exists.
Q2. Two nearby APs use channels 1 and 3. Is that better or worse than both using channel 1?
Answer: Usually worse - They cannot defer to each other, so they collide.
Q3. How far apart are 5 GHz channels 36 and 40?
Answer: 20 MHz - The book's 10 MHz claim is wrong (script checked).
Q4. Which band has more non-overlapping channels?
Answer: 5 GHz - Also less crowded.
The idea in plain words. An electrical signal is sent to an antenna and radiated as a wave. The wave repeats in cycles. These properties decide how far and how well your Wi-Fi works. BOOK p569
| Term | Meaning | Why it matters |
| Frequency | Cycles per second. 1 Hz = once per second; 1 MHz = a million; 1 GHz = a billion | Decides the band (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz) |
| Wavelength | Distance from one peak to the next. Shorter wavelength = higher frequency | Decides how obstacles affect the signal |
| Amplitude | Strength of the signal (height of the wave) | More amplitude = stronger signal |
| Gain | An increase in the signal. Active gain = more power from the radio; passive gain = from the antenna shape | More range |
| Attenuation | Natural weakening of the signal with distance | Why signals fade |
EXAM CRITICAL

Lower frequencies travel farther but carry less bandwidth. Higher frequencies travel less far but carry more bandwidth. So 2.4 GHz reaches farther than 5 GHz, and 5 GHz is faster over a shorter distance. BOOK p571
WARNING
Amplifiers can distort the signal or overload and damage a receiver if you push in too much power. BOOK p572
The decibel and dBm: a short lesson the book promises and skips [ADDED]
The book says it will explain dBm "in more detail soon" but does not. dBm means decibels relative to 1 milliwatt. It is on a logarithmic scale, so small changes mean big power differences. ADDED
| dBm | Power | Meaning |
| 30 dBm | 1000 mW (1 W) | Very strong transmit power |
| 20 dBm | 100 mW | Typical strong AP transmit power |
| 0 dBm | 1 mW | The reference point |
| -30 dBm | 0.001 mW | Excellent received signal |
| -67 dBm | 0.0000002 mW | A common minimum for good voice and video CHECK |
| -90 dBm | 0.000000001 mW | Close to unusable |
MEMORY TIP

Rules of thumb: +3 dB roughly doubles the power; -3 dB halves it; +10 dB multiplies it by 10; -10 dB divides by 10. Script check: 3 dB = x1.995, 10 dB = x10. A signal at -50 dBm is far stronger than one at -80 dBm; closer to zero is stronger. ADDED
19.5.1 Radio Frequency Behaviors
RF waves do not just travel in a straight line. Seven behaviors affect Wi-Fi. Use this table first, then read each. BOOK p572
| Behavior | What happens | Effect on Wi-Fi |
| Free space path loss | Signal weakens with distance, no obstacle needed | Limits range |
| Absorption | Signal passes through an object and loses energy as heat | Weaker signal behind walls |
| Reflection | Signal bounces off a surface | Leads to multipath |
| Multipath | Reflected copies arrive later and out of phase | Downfade, nulls or upfade |
| Refraction | Signal bends when passing between different media (for example dry to humid air) | Mostly outdoor long links |
| Diffraction | Signal bends around an object | Dead spots behind buildings |
| Scattering | Signal breaks into many unpredictable directions (dust, rain, leaves) | Unpredictable loss |
19.5.2 Free Space Path Loss

The signal weakens as it spreads out, even with no obstacles. Two things on each end decide the effect: the signal strength given to the antenna (active gain) and the antenna type (passive gain). A directional antenna focuses the same energy in one direction and so travels farther. The receiver also has a received sensitivity (how weak a signal it can still understand). BOOK pp572-573
VERIFY

Script check (free space path loss formula, general knowledge CHECK ). At 10 m the loss is 60.2 dB at 2.4 GHz and 66.7 dB at 5 GHz, about 6.5 dB more at 5 GHz. Doubling the distance adds about 6 dB at either frequency. This matches the rule: higher frequency, shorter range. ADDED
19.5.3 Absorption

Walls, ceilings, trees, people and cars absorb some energy, so the signal comes out weaker (lower amplitude). Drywall absorbs less than concrete, and some materials block the signal completely. A site survey finds the problem spots and the best AP positions. BOOK pp573-574
19.5.4 Reflection

When a signal strikes an object at an angle, some energy is absorbed and some bounces off at the same angle. How much depends on three things: the angle, the frequency and the nature of the surface. Reflection is the main cause of multipath. BOOK pp574-575
19.5.5 Multipath
Reflected signals take a longer path, so they arrive later and out of phase with the main signal. The result depends on how far out of phase they are: BOOK pp575-576
| Phase difference | Effect | Name |
| About 120 to 170 degrees | Signal is weakened | Downfade |
| 180 degrees | Signals cancel each other | Nulling |
| 360 degrees | Back in phase: signal is boosted | Upfade |
Multipath is usually bad, but 802.11n can use it to get higher speeds (MIMO). BOOK
19.5.6 Refraction

Refraction is a change in direction when a signal passes through different media, mostly dry air to wet air. It matters on long outdoor links. Dry air bends the signal away from the earth; humid air bends it toward the earth. BOOK p576
19.5.7 Diffraction
Diffraction is a signal bending around an object, like water waves around a rock. It creates dead spots behind objects such as buildings. BOOK pp576-577
COMMON MISTAKE

The book ends this section with "diffraction bends the RF, whereas in refraction the RF bounces". That is wrong and it contradicts the book's own definition of refraction. Refraction bends a signal as it passes between media; reflection bounces it; diffraction bends it around an object. UPDATED
19.5.8 Scattering

In scattering, the signal breaks up and bounces in many unpredictable directions. Causes: dust, humidity and rain, rough or uneven surfaces, moving water and tree leaves. Its unpredictability makes it hard to fix. BOOK p577
COMMON MISTAKE
The book says scattering is "a lot like refraction". It is really like reflection, except the signal goes in many directions instead of one. UPDATED
The book repeats that nothing beats a thorough site survey before and after a WLAN design: it finds RF problems, AP positions and antenna types. BOOK p578
19.5.9 RF Operational Requirements
Line of sight [BOOK]

For large areas and outdoor point-to-point bridges, you need RF line of sight, which is not the same as visual line of sight. WLANs use spread spectrum: a "channel 6" signal is spread across 22 MHz, so enough of it must arrive to be understood. Things that block it: mountains, the curvature of the earth, buildings and trees. The book's figure says line of sight disappears at about 6 miles (9.7 km) because of the earth's curve (script check: 6 miles = 9.66 km). BOOK pp578-579
Fresnel zone [BOOK]

The Fresnel zone is a football-shaped (elliptical) area between the transmitter and receiver. It must be at least 60 percent clear for good reception. Even a small blockage, such as tree tops, can hurt the link although visual line of sight looks fine. BOOK p579
VERIFY

Script check (first Fresnel zone radius r = 8.657 x sqrt(distance in km / frequency in GHz) meters, general knowledge CHECK ): a 1 km link at 2.4 GHz has a radius of about 5.6 m at the middle, so keep about 3.4 m (60 percent) clear. At 5 GHz it is 3.9 m, with 2.3 m (60 percent). ADDED
RSSI and SNR [BOOK] p580
| Measure | What it tells you | Good value |
| RSSI | Received signal strength at the receiver. A vendor-defined grade (the book says 0 to 255) that maps to dBm values | Closer to zero dBm is stronger (for example -50 dBm beats -80 dBm) |
| SNR | Signal strength compared with the surrounding RF noise | Higher is better |
- dBm is relative, a value compared with 1 milliwatt. RSSI values from different card vendors cannot be compared because each uses its own scale. BOOK
- If the noise is close to the signal level, the signal cannot be picked out: like whispering in a loud room. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book's statement that RSSI values "are negative" mixes the grade with the dBm value. The grade is a vendor number; the dBm equivalent is negative. UPDATED CHECK
Causes of interference [ADDED]

v2.0 objective 1.5.d asks about the cause of interference. The book only covers other APs on overlapping channels (section 19.4). Common sources: other Wi-Fi networks on the same or adjacent channel (co-channel and adjacent-channel interference), Bluetooth and other 2.4 GHz devices, microwave ovens, cordless phones and baby monitors, and physical obstacles such as metal and concrete. Moving to 5 GHz or choosing a clear channel helps. ADDED CHECK (general knowledge; not looked up)
Quick check 19.5
Q1. Which RF behavior makes reflected signals arrive late and out of phase?
Answer: Multipath (caused by reflection) - Pre-check Q5.
Q2. Signals arrive exactly 180 degrees out of phase. What is the effect?
Answer: Nulling: they cancel each other - 360 degrees gives upfade.
Q3. How much of the Fresnel zone must be clear?
Answer: At least 60 percent - Even if visual line of sight is clear.
Q4. Which is the stronger signal: -55 dBm or -75 dBm?
Answer: -55 dBm - Closer to zero is stronger (script table).
Q5. Does a higher SNR mean a better or worse link?
Answer: Better - More signal compared with noise.
Q6. Which frequency travels farther, 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz?
Answer: 2.4 GHz - Lower frequency travels farther, but with less bandwidth.
Q7. Signal bends around a building and leaves a dead spot behind it. Which behavior?
Answer: Diffraction - Not refraction.

The idea in plain words. Wireless signals go through walls, so anyone nearby can listen. Two jobs protect you: authentication (who are you?) and encryption (scramble the data so a listener cannot read it). The book says the original 802.11 designers did not expect wireless to outnumber wired hosts, so security is basically off by default. BOOK pp549, 581
19.6.1 Authentication and Encryption
The 802.11 committee specified two authentication types: open and shared-key. BOOK p581
| Type | How it works | Verdict |

| Open authentication | The client just supplies the right SSID and the AP says yes. Done at Layer 2 (MAC layer). The most common method | No real authentication. Fine for public hotspots; not for enterprises |

| Shared-key authentication | The AP sends a clear-text challenge. The client encrypts it with its WEP key and returns it | Not secure: an attacker sees the challenge and the encrypted answer and can work out the WEP key. Not used today |
The six steps to join an AP (open authentication) [BOOK]
- The client sends a probe request.
- APs send probe responses. The client picks the best AP.
- The client sends an authentication request to that AP.
- The AP confirms authentication and registers the client.
- The client sends an association request.
- The AP confirms the association.
COMMON MISTAKE

Figure captions in the book are mixed up. Figure 19.30 is called "shared-key authentication" in the text, but its steps are the open process (no challenge). Figure 19.31, whose steps include the challenge text, is captioned "Open access process". The steps themselves are right; ignore the captions. UPDATED
WARNING

All Wi-Fi certified products ship in open access mode with security off, so that anyone can plug in an AP and get online. Never leave defaults on in a business or home network. The authentication here is at Layer 2; stronger higher-layer authentication (802.1X) comes after association. BOOK pp581-582

WEP (Wired Equivalent Privacy) encrypts data with a key of 40 or 128 bits, usually static: you type the same key on the AP and on every client. With WEP, even a client that authenticates and associates cannot send or receive data without the right key. The book's main point: static keys on every device are impossible to manage in a large network. BOOK pp582-583
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

WEP is broken and must not be used. It uses the RC4 cipher with a 24-bit initialization vector (16,777,216 values, script check), and IV reuse lets attackers recover the key. Wi-Fi Alliance moved on to WPA and WPA2. WEP appears in the exam only as the weak, old method. ADDED CHECK (general knowledge; not looked up)
19.6.3 WPA and WPA2: An Overview

WPA was a stopgap from the Wi-Fi Alliance, released before the IEEE finished 802.11i. When 802.11i was ratified, WPA2 included its improvements. WPA could be a software update on old hardware; WPA2 needed newer hardware (now universal). BOOK p583
|  | WPA | WPA2 |
| Based on | Step toward 802.11i | Full 802.11i |
| Encryption | TKIP (RC4) with MIC | AES-CCMP (AES in counter mode with CBC-MAC) |
| Confidentiality and integrity | TKIP and MIC | AES-CCMP gives both |
| Hardware | Software update on WEP hardware | Newer hardware |
Personal (PSK) and Enterprise [BOOK]
| Mode | Authentication | Where used |
| Personal (PSK) | A shared passphrase on the AP and each client. The PSK feeds the key generation | SOHO. In enterprises only for devices that cannot use RADIUS (for example some VoIP phones) |
| Enterprise | IEEE 802.1X / EAP with a RADIUS server. Each user or device is authenticated | Business, education, government |
WARNING
The only known weakness of WPA/WPA2 PSK is a weak passphrase: a dictionary attack can guess it. Use a long, strong passphrase. A lost or stolen client reveals the PSK, like static WEP. BOOK p584
What TKIP added over WEP [BOOK]
- A 48-bit IV instead of 24-bit (script check: 281,474,976,710,656 values; the book says 280 trillion), used in order, so IVs are not reused.
- A new key for every packet (temporal key plus IV plus serial number, with per-packet key hashing).
- Central key management by the AP, with rotating broadcast keys. The PSK is used to derive the PMK, then the PTKs.

- A MIC (message integrity code) instead of a plain frame check sequence. It catches bit-flipping. If the AP sees two MIC failures within 60 seconds it disassociates all stations and stops traffic for 60 seconds.
The key steps in WPA2-Enterprise [BOOK] p585
- The authentication server and the station each derive the PMK (Pairwise Master Key). It stays the same for the whole session. The server passes it to the AP.

- The four-way handshake between AP and station derives the PTK (Pairwise Transient Key): (1) the AP sends a random ANonce; (2) the station replies with its SNonce plus a MIC; (3) the AP sends a group key (GTK) and confirms the security parameters; (4) the station confirms the keys are installed.
- The handshake also confirms that both peers are still alive.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's wording for message 2 ("a key used to encrypt a nonce") is loose. The PTK is derived from the PMK, both nonces and both MAC addresses; the station sends its SNonce with a MIC for integrity. For the exam, remember the names and the order: PMK first, then the four-way handshake, then the PTK. UPDATED CHECK
802.11i additions [BOOK] p585
- A list of allowed EAP methods.
- AES-CCMP instead of RC4.
- Better key management: the master key can be cached, so a station reconnects faster.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
TKIP is deprecated and WPA is obsolete. Most current networks should use WPA2 with AES (CCMP) or WPA3. A network that offers TKIP will not satisfy WPA3. ADDED CHECK

The Wi-Fi Alliance announced WPA3 in 2018 to replace WPA2 (which dates from 2004). Like WPA2, it has Personal and Enterprise versions. Rules shared by all WPA3 networks: use the latest security methods, no outdated legacy protocols, and Protected Management Frames (PMF) required. BOOK p586
WPA3-Personal [BOOK] pp586-587

- Uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), also called the Dragonfly handshake, instead of WPA2's PSK exchange. It forces live interaction on each login, so an attacker cannot grab a hash and crack it offline with a dictionary attack. This is the answer to "built-in resistance to dictionary attacks" (review question 8).
- Natural password selection: users can pick passwords that are easier to remember.
- Ease of use: same way of connecting as before.
- Forward secrecy: traffic recorded earlier stays protected even if the password is later compromised.
WPA3-Enterprise [BOOK] p587
- Improves WPA2-Enterprise with a stronger option: a 192-bit security mode.
- The book's list for that mode: GCMP-256 encryption, HMAC-SHA384 key derivation, ECDH and ECDSA with a 384-bit curve, and BIP-GMAC-256 management frame protection.

- OWE (Opportunistic Wireless Encryption) improves open networks: encryption with no password, a unique key for every device (Individualized Data Protection). This is the answer to review question 12 (not "OWL").
- The book also mentions DPP (Device Provisioning Protocol) to add devices by NFC tag or QR code.
COMMON MISTAKE

GCMP-256 is not the standard WPA3-Enterprise cipher. The Wi-Fi Alliance says standard WPA3-Enterprise requires at least AES-CCMP-128 (with BIP-CMAC-128 for management frames); GCMP-256 and BIP-GMAC-256 belong to the optional 192-bit mode. The book's Table 19.1 and review question 1 give GCMP-256 for WPA3-Enterprise. For the exam, with those answer choices, GCMP-256 is the expected answer; in real life know the 192-bit distinction. UPDATED (wi-fi.org, official; also vendor documentation)
DPP is sold by the Wi-Fi Alliance as Wi-Fi Easy Connect and is a separate program, not a WPA3 requirement. UPDATED CHECK

The book calls WPA3 "upgraded to 128-bit encryption" and warns about Dragonblood, a set of early attacks on WPA3 including downgrade to WPA2 in transition mode. Treat the details as history; fixes and updated certifications followed. CHECK
WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 compared (book Table 19.1) [BOOK] [UPDATED]
| Mode | WPA | WPA2 | WPA3 |
| Enterprise authentication | 802.1X / EAP | 802.1X / EAP | 802.1X / EAP |
| Enterprise encryption | TKIP / MIC | AES-CCMP | GCMP-256 (192-bit mode); standard WPA3-Enterprise: at least AES-CCMP 128 |
| Personal authentication | PSK | PSK | SAE |
| Personal encryption | TKIP / MIC | AES-CCMP | AES-CCMP |
| Cipher family | 128-bit RC4 with TKIP | 128-bit AES | 128-bit AES (192-bit mode available) |
| Ad hoc | Not supported | Not supported | Not supported |
EXAM CRITICAL

One-line memory: WEP = RC4, weak. WPA = TKIP. WPA2 = AES-CCMP. WPA3 = SAE (Personal), GCMP-256 (192-bit Enterprise), OWE for open networks, PMF required. RC4 is used by WEP and TKIP (review question 15).
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

The book's Exam Essentials has a garbled last line ("Understand the difference between WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 802.11n uses 40.") and no explanation of the differences. The table above replaces it. UPDATED
Quick check 19.6
Q1. Which authentication type is most common and sends no credentials, only the SSID?
Answer: Open authentication - Done at Layer 2.
Q2. Which two encryption methods are based on RC4?
Answer: WEP and TKIP - AES-CCMP replaced RC4.
Q3. What does the four-way handshake produce?
Answer: The PTK (Pairwise Transient Key) - The PMK exists before the handshake.
Q4. Which WPA3 feature stops offline dictionary attacks?
Answer: SAE (Dragonfly handshake) - It forces interaction on every login attempt.
Q5. What does OWE give an open network?
Answer: Encryption with a unique key per device, no password - It replaces plain open authentication.
Q6. How many MIC failures within 60 seconds make a TKIP AP shut traffic down?
Answer: Two (traffic stops for 60 seconds) - Stops key-recovery attacks.

The book has no troubleshooting section for this chapter, so this section is added. The v2.0 outline (1.6) asks you to troubleshoot wireless client connectivity, including wireless security parameters. ADDED CHECK (not tested on hardware)
| Symptom | Likely cause | First check |
| Client cannot see the SSID | Hidden SSID; client does not support the band; wrong regional channel (for example a DFS channel) | Add the SSID manually; check band and channel settings |
| Client sees SSID but cannot join | Wrong passphrase; security mismatch (WPA2 vs WPA3, TKIP vs AES); PMF required but not supported | Compare security type, cipher and passphrase on client and AP |
| Joins but has no IP address | DHCP problem or wrong VLAN on the AP port | Check the DHCP scope, the SSID-to-VLAN mapping and the switchport |
| Slow, dropping connection | Weak signal (low RSSI), low SNR, co-channel or adjacent-channel interference, too many clients | Check the signal, channel plan (1, 6, 11) and neighbors |
| Drops when walking between APs | Too little cell overlap; different SSID or security on the APs; same channel on neighbors | Check SSID, security, channels and overlap (15 to 20 percent) |
| Old device cannot connect | Network is WPA3-only or does not allow TKIP or old 802.11b rates | Use WPA2/WPA3 transition mode or update the device |

| Review question 13 case: b/g client, no clients listed on the AP | Client SSID is wrong (the AP never sees an association). A wrong PSK would still show the client attempting | Check the SSID name and spelling on the client first |

content.text: Run in Command Prompt (Windows) ADDED CHECK
netsh wlan show interfaces
netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid
- netsh wlan show interfaces - details about the network you are connected to: SSID, BSSID, radio type, authentication, cipher, channel, signal.
- netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid - every visible network with each BSSID, channel, signal percentage and authentication.

- Run the first command. Write down the SSID, BSSID, radio type (for example 802.11ac or 802.11ax), channel, authentication (WPA2-Personal, WPA3-Personal ...) and cipher (CCMP ...). Expected: authentication and cipher match what your router is set to. CHECK

- Run the second command. Count how many neighbor networks use your channel. Expected: in a busy area several use 1, 6 or 11 on 2.4 GHz. This is co-channel interference in real life. CHECK

- Note the signal percentage. Windows shows a percentage, not dBm. A commonly quoted rough conversion is dBm = (percentage / 2) minus 100, so 100 percent is about -50 dBm. Treat it as approximate. CHECK
- Walk to another room and run the first command again. Expected: lower signal and sometimes a different BSSID if you have several APs (roaming within one ESS, same SSID). CHECK

labs.title: SOHO wireless router with WPA2 (Packet Tracer)

content.text: - Place a Wireless Router (such as WRT300N), one Laptop and one PC. Replace the laptop's wired module with a wireless module (power the laptop off, swap the module, power on). CHECK
- Open the router's GUI tab: Wireless > Basic Wireless Settings. Set SSID LabNet, standard mixed or N, channel 1. Expected: the laptop's PC Wireless app lists LabNet. CHECK
- Wireless > Wireless Security: choose WPA2 Personal, encryption AES, passphrase Lab-pass-2026. Save. Expected: the router now asks for the passphrase. CHECK
- On the laptop connect to LabNet with that passphrase. Expected: the laptop gets an IP address by DHCP (the router has a DHCP server) and can ping the router. CHECK

- Break it: change the passphrase on the laptop. Expected: it cannot connect. Fix it. Then set the SSID differently on the laptop profile to see the "not found" failure. This models review question 13. CHECK
- Try choosing WPA3 or SAE. Expected: Packet Tracer may not offer it. That is a simulator limit, not a rule. CHECK
- Connect a switch to a router and two AccessPoint-PT devices (both on the switch). Place a laptop between them. CHECK
- On both APs set the same SSID Corp and the same security (WPA2-PSK, AES, same passphrase). Set different channels: AP1 on 1, AP2 on 6. Expected: the laptop connects to the nearer AP. CHECK

- Move the laptop closer to the other AP. Expected: it re-associates with the other AP while keeping the same IP (roaming inside one ESS). Packet Tracer shows association in the PC Wireless app. CHECK

- Questions to answer in your notes: why different channels? Why the same SSID and security? How much should the cells overlap? (see section 19.3.5). Packet Tracer does not model interference, so you will not see slowdowns from same-channel placement. CHECK
A Python script you can run in VS Code ADDED
import math
def mw(dbm): return 10 ** (dbm / 10)
def fspl(d_m, f_mhz): return 20*math.log10(d_m/1000) + 20*math.log10(f_mhz) + 32.44
print(mw(20), mw(-67))
print(round(fspl(10, 2437),1), round(fspl(10, 5180),1))
print(round(8.657*math.sqrt(1/2.4),2))
- mw(dbm) - converts dBm to milliwatts. 20 dBm = 100 mW; -67 dBm = 0.0000002 mW.
- fspl(...) - free space path loss in dB for a distance in meters and a frequency in MHz.
- 8.657*sqrt(D/f) - first Fresnel zone radius in meters for a link of D km at f GHz.

Expected output (from my own run of the same formulas): 100.0 1.995e-07 (Python prints more digits), then 60.2 66.7, then 5.59. If your numbers differ, check your formula. Then answer: how much extra loss does 5 GHz have over 2.4 GHz? (about 6.5 dB) What does doubling the distance cost? (about 6 dB). CHECK

content.text: Q1 Which wireless network type is Bluetooth?
Answer: WPAN - Personal area network.
Q2 Why is a WLAN compared to Ethernet with hubs?
Answer: It is half-duplex: all devices share one channel and only one transmits at a time - A switch gives each port its own collision domain; an AP does not.
Q3 Which wireless type needs line of sight between sites?
Answer: WMAN (wireless bridges between buildings) - Fiber is better if available.
Q4 Do WLAN users pay to use the radio frequency band?
Answer: No, it is an unlicensed band - Same for PANs.
Q1 What is the wired side of an AP called?
Answer: The distribution system (DS) - It also carries MAC information for the 802.11 frames.
Q2 Which type of AP gets its configuration from a WLC?
Answer: Lightweight AP - Autonomous APs are configured individually.
Q3 Which antenna type usually gives the longest range in one direction?
Answer: D - irectional (Yagi) - It focuses the power.
Q4 Why do most APs use omni antennas?
Answer: C - lients can be in any direction - A directional antenna would miss most of them.
Q1 Two laptops connect directly with no AP. What is this topology called?
Answer: IBSS (ad hoc) - Review question 16 in the book.
Q2 How long can an SSID be?
Answer: 1 to 32 octets (up to 32 characters) - The book: sequence of 1 to 32 octets.
Q3 Why create several SSIDs on one AP?
Answer: To give different groups different security settings - It does not improve performance.
Q4 To let users roam without disconnecting, what must be true of the SSID and the channels?
Answer: Same SSID on all APs, different channels on neighboring APs - That creates an ESS.
Q5 How much throughput does each repeater cost?
Answer: A - bout half - Use repeaters only for low-bandwidth devices.
Q6 Can two root bridges talk to each other?
Answer: No - Root devices only talk to non-root devices.
Q1 Which 2.4 GHz channels are non-overlapping in the US?
Answer: 1, 6 and 11 - Script check: no set of four exists.
Q2 Two nearby APs use channels 1 and 3. Is that better or worse than both using channel 1?
Answer: Usually worse - They cannot defer to each other, so they collide.
Q3 How far apart are 5 GHz channels 36 and 40?
Answer: 20 MHz - The book's 10 MHz claim is wrong (script checked).
Q4 Which band has more non-overlapping channels?
Answer: 5 GHz - Also less crowded.

Answer: Multipath (caused by reflection) - Pre-check Q5.
Q2 Signals arrive exactly 180 degrees out of phase. What is the effect?

Answer: B - Higher frequency travels less far but gives more usable channels.

A. WEP
B. TKIP
C. AES
D. CCMP
Answer: A - , B - AES-CCMP replaced RC4.
Q18 Which encryption does WPA2 use?
A. TKIP/MIC
B. AES-CCMP
C. RC4
D. SAE
Answer: B - SAE is the WPA3-Personal handshake.

Answer: PMK before; PTK from the handshake - The handshake uses ANonce and SNonce.

B. AES

Answer: C - Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (Dragonfly).

Answer: Protected Management Frames (PMF) - Required in WPA3.
Q23 Choose two statements that describe WPA.
A. Dynamic encryption keys change during the connection

C. It can use PSK authentication
D. Static WEP keys are required
Answer: A - , C - Book question 17.
Q24 Why would an administrator create several SSIDs on one AP?
Answer: To give different groups different security settings - It does not add speed.
Q25 What three things make roaming work well inside a building?
Answer: Same SSID and security on the APs, different channels on neighbors, 15 to 20 percent cell overlap - The book gives 20 percent in text and 15 percent in a question.
Q26 A client with a b/g card cannot join an 802.11b/g AP, and the AP lists no clients at all. What is a likely reason?
A. Wrong channel set on the client
B. Wrong IP subnet
C. Wrong pre-shared key
D. Wrong SSID on the client
Answer: D - The AP only lists clients that associate. A wrong IP or key would still show an association attempt. A client usually scans all channels itself. CHECK

Answer: Other APs on the same or adjacent channel, microwave ovens, Bluetooth and cordless phones - v2.0 objective 1.5.d. CHECK

Answer: No - The name still appears in some frames; use encryption instead.
